We took images of dilute GFP or autofluorescent Luria Broth (LB) to correct for uneven illumination in the imaging plane. The exposure time and laser power both scaled linearly on our instrument (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) which allowed us to adjust for dimmer or brighter signals by changing the exposure time.

#### Cryo-electron tomography sample preparation

Holey carbon grids (Quantifoil R2/1, 200 mesh, gold) were glow discharged using a Pelco SC-6 sputter coater and sterilized in 70% ethanol in H2O. SK-MEL-2 cells were plated in DMEM/F12 (Gibco) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (premium grade, VWR Seradigm Life Science) and 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin (Gibco) onto grids and incubated overnight at 37°C and 5% CO2 in a cell culture incubator. Samples were blotted and plunge frozen using a Vitrobot Mark IV (FEI) after addition of 10 nm BSA Gold Tracer (Electron Microscopy Sciences).

#### Cryo-electron tomography data recording and processing

Tilt-series were recorded on a Titan Krios operated at 300 kV (FEI) equipped with a Quantum energy filter (Gatan) and a K2 direct electron detecting device (Gatan) at 2.97 Å pixel size and a target defocus of −2 µm. SerialEM (Mastronarde, 2005) in low-dose mode was used for automated tilt series acquisition using a bidirectional tilt scheme covering a whole tilt range from +60° to −60° with a base increment of 2° and a total electron dose of 100e-/Å2. Tomograms were generated in IMOD (Kremer et al., 1996) using the gold beads as fiducials for tilt-series alignment. For Figure 5, tomograms were reconstructed using the ﻿simultaneous iterative reconstruction technique (SIRT) reconstruction algorithm, then filtered using the Nonlinear Anisotropic Diffusion (NAD) filter in IMOD and binned by a factor of 2. For Figure 5—video 1, we used the backprojection algorithm for tomogram reconstruction followed by a smoothing filter (Clip smooth function in IMOD). The U-shaped pit shown is one of six sites of CME we have identified in our tomograms, all of which have bent actin filaments around the pit to varying degrees. The bent filaments are especially prominent in the tomogram shown because of the orientation of the pit with respect to the missing wedge effect. A detailed treatment of these tomograms will be the subject of a subsequent study.

### Data analysis

Calibration curve: We used a combination of custom-written and publicly available image analysis software in Fiji (1.52i) and Matlab (r2017b) to analyze the traces of fluorescence intensity per spot, for multiple Z slices and time points. To measure fluorescence intensity per spot of GFP-tagged nanocages, we wrote a toolset in Fiji to select and circular regions of interest eight pixels (1.1 µm) in diameter, and used cross-correlation to center the regions around the intensity-based center of mass. We selected as background regions of concentric circles one pixel larger than the original region of interest. The toolset measured the fluorescence intensity per spot, which we subtracted by the area-corrected background intensity to yield fluorescence intensity per spot for the four constructs. Some analysis functions were adapted from published software (Akamatsu et al., 2017; Epstein et al., 2018; McCormick et al., 2013). We measured only spots that were contained within the slices imaged and were single stationary spots. For comparison of fluorescence to eGFP-MotB, we used smaller (6-pixel) ROIs.

We plotted background-subtracted fluorescence intensity per spot as a function of predicted copy number per structure to obtain a calibration curve relating fluorescence intensity per spot to numbers of molecules per structure. For the curve in Figure 3D, we combined data from three experiments with different imaging conditions by defining the average 60mer-GFP intensity per experiment as 1000 arbitrary units. Lines are linear fits through zero with r2 calculated by linear least-squares fitting.

Time-lapse fluorescence quantification: We made modifications to automated MATLAB-based tracking software (Aguet et al., 2013; Hong et al., 2015) to track and analyze fluorescence-intensity time lapse data of genome-edited cells. The core tracking program (based on the software package µ-track) automatically identifies fluorescent spots and connects them as tracks by minimizing the linear assignment problem (Jaqaman et al., 2008). We used stringent tracking parameters with gap size 0 and search radius 0–2.3 pixels (248 nm). GFP and RFP tracks with high variability in the intensity/time profile were automatically rejected (Ferguson et al., 2017) as well as tracks ≤ 3 s in duration (Dambournet et al., 2018) and the remaining tracks were associated spatiotemporally according to a cost matrix (Hong et al., 2015). We used two track rejection schemes. In the first, users were presented with fluorescence montages and XY coordinates of the tracks to assess the fidelity of tracking for each event (Hong et al., 2015). In the second, tracks were automatically rejected based signal-to-noise ratio (>1.05) and proximity to neighboring tracks (>525 nm) (Hong et al., 2015). We checked that the manual and automatic track rejection schemes yielded similar results (lifetime distributions and intensity versus time plots) as well as to manual, kymograph-based quantification of lifetimes (below). From the above workflow (Dambournet et al., 2018) we increased throughput by connecting all steps into an automated tracking pipeline requiring minimal user input. For SK-MEL-2 cells expressing CLTA-RFP and DNM2-GFP, we tracked regions that were not near the nucleus (which has a concentration of Golgi-derived clathrin budding) and that did not have large, bright, persistent structures containing invariant RFP and GFP signals (‘plaques,’ which are likely sites of adhesion).

Alignment method: For Figure 2G, we aligned tracks based on the time point after the peak intensity in which 50% of the fluorescence remained in the GFP channel. We normalized the fluorescence intensity to compare movies from different imaging conditions. For Figure 2I, we aligned the tracks based on the maximum intensity. For Figure 6D, we aligned the tracks based on the disappearance of the RFP signal. This code is available at the following website: https://github.com/DrubinBarnes/Akamatsu_CME_manuscript.

Manual track analysis: We wrote a Fiji toolset that generated two-color kymographs from user-defined regions of interest, and then quantified the lifetime based on the lengths of the kymographs (from user-defined regions on the kymographs). This manual analysis was used in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and for verification of the automated tracking scheme. This code is available at the following website: https://github.com/DrubinBarnes/Akamatsu_CME_manuscript.

Nanocage particle tracking: To track the membrane-tethered nanocages in 2D in cells we used TrackMate, a plugin available in Fiji that optimizes the Linear Assignment Problem (LAP) (Jaqaman et al., 2008). We detected spots using an estimate of 0.5 µm and threshold of 15, using a median filter and sub-pixel localization. We used the simple LAP tracker with a maximum linking and gap closing distance of 1 µm and two frames and a minimum track length of 4 frames.

Calculating numbers of molecules per endocytic site: We calculated the fluorescence intensity of background-subtracted ArpC3-GFP spots colocalized with AP2-RFP spots from single time-point images using the same background correction approach described for the calibration curve. We used the slope of the calibration curve to convert fluorescence intensity to numbers of molecules of ArpC3-GFP. Because the standard is inside cells, this standard controls for fluorescence environment and fluorescent protein folding and maturation. We used the resultant histogram of numbers of ArpC3-GFP per spot and the time-lapse fluorescence intensity data in Figure 2G to create the graph in Figure 2I of numbers of molecules of ArpC3-GFP over time.

Acceptance summary:

How actin polymerization generates forces during clathrin-mediated endocytosis in mammalian cells is still not clear. This work combines simulations of actin filaments and continuous modeling of membrane mechanics with high resolution experiments in living cells in order to study the self-organization of actin filaments during endocytosis. The number of Arp2/3 complexes (involved in branched actin network formation) has been measured in genome-edited human living cells and directly used in the simulations. The paper predicts that self-organization of actin filaments around the clathrin pit should produce enough force to pull on the bud in normal tension conditions, and to adapt to mechanical changes. It also predicts that some actin filaments should be bent, which was confirmed by cryoEM on intact cells, as well as how endocytosis should be quantitatively altered by molecular components involved in the process. Globally, this work should provide a solid basis for future quantitative studies to establish a molecular model of endocytosis.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Principles of self-organization and load adaptation by the actin cytoskeleton during clathrin-mediated endocytosis" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, including Patricia Bassereau as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by Vivek Malhotra as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Alex Mogilner (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

We have some concerns that should be addressed or at least discussed in a revised version of the manuscript.

1) On a general ground, considering the modeling, the mechanical contribution to endocytosis of the membrane and of the rest of the system is included in an elastic force that opposes to the actin-driven deformation. However, in mammalian cells, budding happens very often independently of actin; many proteins are involved in budding before dynamin scission, producing elongation and bending forces on the membrane, thus favoring deformation, not the opposite. This is a key difference that should be justified at least.

2) Some initial assumptions about the initial localization of the NPF or Arp2/3, or the initiation of actin from small fragments on the coat should also be justified and the robustness of the model to these hypotheses should also be checked

3) The only direct testing of the prediction of the model is the observation of bent actin filaments around a bud. First, a clear evidence of the clathrin-related nature of the bud should be provided. Moreover, the simulations make many more predictions about the effect of certain parameters on internalization. It would reinforce the work if more critical tests of the model could be performed to confirm its validity, for instance, changing the density of actin nucleators, the capping rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) or the density of Hip1R (Figure 4) should have a strong effect, while changing the density of Arp2/3 should not (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

Your revised article has been evaluated by Vivek Malhotra as the Senior Editor, a Reviewing Editor and two reviewers.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

Reviewer #2

1) Results subsection “Multiscale modeling shows that a minimal branched actin network is sufficient to internalize endocytic pits against physiological membrane tension “: '[…] direct scaling between resistance to internalization and membrane tension allowed us to treat this step of endocytic pit internalization as a linear spring […] ' – by internalization, do you mean some linear distance? Why does the force scale linearly with distance? (For example, force to push filopodia is constant, independent of the length…)

2) From the figures in which snapshots from the simulations are shown, it looks like an awful lot of filaments grows away from the pit, kind of contradicting the conclusions. Plates of the figures showing actin densities are hard to interpret. Basically, the authors need to think how to convey more convincingly the conclusion that the actin network is focused – at least, I could not convince myself that I see this from the simulation-generated data…

3) Readers need physical and geometric intuition about the results, and the text is a bit weak in that regard. When revising, pay attention at instances like 'simulations showed that…', and then the text goes to the next point – we need to understand qualitatively why the result is what it is.

Reviewer #3:

1) It would be very helpful to know the actual percentage of clathrin coated pits associated with bent actin filaments in their electron tomograms. It will help to grasp the actual contribution of actin filament bending on force generation.

2) It is still confusing when they talk about activated Arp2/3 complex, when they actually mean activated N-WASP. In essence, the Arp2/3 complex still attached to the actin branches is active too, and the authors do not really know where this pool of Arp2/3 is located. As they mention in the respond to the reviewer, what it is known in mammalian cells is the localization of N-WASP (presumably active) and not the position of the active Arp2/3 complex.

results.result: A minimal branched actin network with approximately 200 Arp2/3 complexes is sufficient to internalize endocytic pits up to ~60 nm against physiological membrane tension. The model is robust to variations in filament stiffness, stall force, and Hip1R affinity, but is particularly sensitive to the number of Arp2/3 complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C19, C20, and C21 are supported by computational simulations (Figure 1F-G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing that the minimal actin network can drive internalization and that Arp2/3 complex number is a critical parameter. The model predictions are constrained by experimental parameters and show consistent internalization outcomes across parameter sweeps.

results.result: A newly developed molecule-counting method using GFP-tagged nanocages as calibration standards determined that approximately 200 Arp2/3 complexes accumulate at sites of clathrin-mediated endocytosis in human induced pluripotent stem cells. The vast majority (81 ± 10%) of CME events show ArpC3-GFP bursts prior to internalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C22, C23, C25, C66, and C84 are supported by experimental data including calibration curves (Figure 2D, R² = 0.996), time-lapse imaging (Figure 2G), and molecule counting (Figure 2I). The method is validated by showing linear proportionality between fluorescence and molecule number, and by demonstrating that double-tagged cells have twice the fluorescence of single-tagged cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-D). Claim C83 provides structural justification for the tagging strategy.

results.result: Simulations predict that actin self-organizes into a radial dendritic network with barbed ends oriented toward the base of the pit, driving assembly of 150 ± 30 filaments containing 5700 ± 1100 monomers. The network internalizes the pit ~60 nm in 10-15 s, with more barbed ends (10 ± 4) near the base than the neck (1 ± 1), producing an axial force.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C26-C33, and C67 are supported by simulation results (Figure 3A-I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showing the spatial organization, filament numbers, and force production. The self-organization emerges from the model's spatial boundary conditions (Arp2/3 at base, Hip1R on coat) and is consistent across multiple simulations (n=96). The prediction of axial force production (C33) follows logically from the spatial distribution of barbed ends.

results.result: The surface distribution of Hip1R around the endocytic pit strongly impacts endocytic outcome, with both rate and extent of internalization increasing with Hip1R coverage. A threshold of ~100 Hip1R molecules is necessary for internalization. In contrast, varying Arp2/3 complex surface density by 20-fold or localizing some Arp2/3 at the neck had little impact.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C40, C72, and C74 are supported by systematic simulation studies (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplements 1-3) showing that Hip1R distribution is critical while Arp2/3 density is not. The mechanism is explained by Hip1R coverage directing more barbed ends toward the base (C38), which increases Arp2/3 binding (C39) and filament nucleation. The threshold of ~100 Hip1R molecules (C40) is clearly demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

results.result: Long actin filaments bend between attachment sites in the coat and the base of the pit, storing elastic energy. Simulations show 13 ± 3% of filaments bend beyond thermal fluctuations, storing up to ~750 pN·nm of elastic energy—larger than the work required for internalization. Cryo-electron tomography confirms the presence of bent filaments at endocytic sites in SK-MEL-2 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C41-C50, and C68 are supported by both simulation data (Figure 5A, E-F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and experimental validation via cryo-electron tomography (Figure 5B). The simulations quantify bending energy and show it exceeds internalization work requirements (C46), while remaining below filament severing thresholds (C44). The experimental observation of bent filaments at endocytic sites (C42) validates a key model prediction.

results.result: Elastic energy stored in bent filaments contributes to endocytic internalization. When membrane tension is released in simulations, pit internalization sharply increases while filament bending near the base decreases by 50%, consistent with energy release supporting internalization through an elastic Brownian ratchet mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C51, C52, C6, and C77 are supported by simulation experiments where tension is released at t=10s (Figure 5G-I, Figure 5—video 2). The sharp increase in internalization (C51) coupled with gradual decrease in bending energy (C52) demonstrates that stored elastic energy can drive internalization. The mechanism is consistent with elastic Brownian ratchet theory (C77), supported by citations to theoretical work.

results.result: Inhibiting Arp2/3 complex activity stalls endocytosis. Simulations predict that nucleation rates below 1 filament per second inhibit endocytosis, which was validated experimentally by treating SK-MEL-2 cells with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK-666, resulting in dose-dependent and time-dependent inhibition of endocytic progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by both simulation predictions (Figure 6A-B) and experimental validation (Figure 6C-D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A). The simulations identify a threshold nucleation rate of 1 filament per second (C54, consistent with Beltzner and Pollard 2008), and CK-666 treatment experiments confirm dose-dependent inhibition of endocytosis (C55), validating the model prediction.

results.result: The endocytic actin network adapts to changes in membrane tension. Under elevated tension, more growing filaments are directed toward the base of the pit, increasing Arp2/3 recruitment, actin nucleation, and filament bending. At >50x higher tension (1 pN/nm), internalization slows but is not abolished, with the network showing better performance than expected for a non-adapting system.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9, C56-C61, and C69 are supported by systematic simulations varying membrane tension (Figure 7A-H, Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The data show tension-dependent attenuation (C56) consistent with prior work, but also demonstrate adaptive behavior (C57) with increased barbed ends at the base (C7, C60), more Arp2/3 binding (C8, C60), more filaments (C60), and increased bending energy (C9, C60) under high tension. The increased energy efficiency (C61) supports the adaptation mechanism.

results.result: The endocytic actin network's ability to adapt to load depends on Hip1R coverage around the pit. A phase diagram shows that cells with high membrane tension are especially sensitive to Arp2/3 nucleation rate, while cells with low tension can perform endocytosis even with low Arp2/3 activity. As Hip1R coverage increases, the network's adaptive capacity increases.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C65 are supported by systematic simulations varying both tension and Hip1R coverage (Figure 8B-G). The phase diagram (Figure 8B) clearly shows differential sensitivity to Arp2/3 activity at different tensions (C62, C63), consistent with experimental observations (Boulant et al., 2011). The dependence of adaptation on Hip1R coverage (C64, C65) is demonstrated by measurements of barbed ends, Arp2/3 binding, filament numbers, and bending energy (Figure 8D-G).

results.result: Membrane mechanics simulations show that a clathrin-coated pit experiences a nearly linear force-extension relationship until ~100 nm internalization, with resistance to internalization directly proportional to plasma membrane tension for a wide range of coat rigidities.
results.evaluation: Claims C17 and C18 are supported by continuum mechanics simulations (Figure 1C-D) showing the linear force-extension regime and the proportionality between resistance and tension. This relationship justifies the simplified spring model used in the actin simulations and is consistent across different coat rigidities.

results.result: Prior experimental work supports the model's predictions: knocking down Hip1R in HeLa cells inhibited endocytosis, and capping actin filament elongation with Cytochalasin inhibits CME.
results.evaluation: Claims C70 and C71 are supported by citations to published literature (Engqvist-Goldstein et al., 2004; Brady et al., 2010; Grassart et al., 2014). These prior results are consistent with the model's predictions about the importance of Hip1R and actin elongation for endocytosis, providing validation for the model's assumptions.

results.result: Based on the relative positions of Arp2/3 activators and Hip1R linkers, the self-organized actin network produces force orthogonal to the base of the pit rather than pinching the neck. The broad Hip1R distribution directs filaments toward the base, nucleating more filaments and increasing bending. Filament bending occurs to a greater extent and longer duration than at flat surfaces, possibly due to curved geometry.
results.evaluation: Claims C73, C75, C78, and C79 are supported by simulation results (Figures 3-5, 7) and represent mechanistic interpretations of the data. The orthogonal force production (C73) is demonstrated in Figure 3I. The role of Hip1R distribution (C79) is shown in Figures 4-5, 7. The comparison to flat surfaces (C78) is an inference supported by the simulation data showing sustained bending. These interpretations are logical and well-supported by the computational results.

results.result: Bent filaments are predicted to contribute to endocytosis resilience by preventing backsliding and by releasing stored elastic energy through thermal fluctuations, consistent with the elastic Brownian ratchet mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C76 and C77 are supported by simulation results (Figure 5) and theoretical considerations. C76 is explicitly stated as a prediction/speculation, while C77 is supported by the tension-release experiments (Figure 5H-I) and is consistent with established theory (De La Cruz and Gardel, 2015a; Mogilner and Oster, 1996). The mechanisms are plausible and supported by the data, though C76 remains a prediction requiring further testing.

results.result: Comparison to yeast endocytosis: An agent-based model of yeast predicted radial filament organization in the XY plane, but the >200x larger force requirements in yeast lead to different axial organization, less filament bending, and a distinct force production mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C80 and C81 are supported by citation to published work on yeast (Mund et al., 2018) and comparison to the current mammalian model. The inference about different mechanisms (C81) is reasonable given the vastly different force scales (turgor pressure in yeast vs. membrane tension in mammalian cells). This comparison contextualizes the current findings within the broader field.

results.result: Background context on actin and endocytosis: Branched actin networks drive membrane forward during cell migration on large scales and deform membranes on smaller scales. In CME, clathrin and BAR proteins generate initial curvature, while actin provides force for membrane shape changes, particularly under high tension where pits stall without functional actin.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C16 are supported by citations to published literature and represent established background knowledge. These claims provide context for the current study and are well-supported by the cited references. They establish the scientific foundation for investigating actin's role in mammalian endocytosis.

results.result: Model parameters are derived from published literature: Arp2/3 branching angle is 77 ± 13°, cytoplasmic actin concentration is 60-100 µM, ATP-actin association rate is 11.6 subunits/µM/s, actin persistence length is 10 µm (flexural rigidity 0.041 pN·µm²), and phalloidin stiffens actin filaments.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C90 are supported by citations to published literature (Blanchoin et al., 2000; Vinzenz et al., 2012; Haugwitz et al., 1994; Wu and Pollard, 2005; Pollard, 1986; McCullough et al., 2008; Gittes et al., 1993; Isambert et al., 1995; Pfaendtner et al., 2010). These parameters are well-established in the literature and provide appropriate constraints for the computational model.
